title: Disciplinary Knowledge 7 Years On
author: Nick Hart
summary: Primary headteacher Nick Hart looks back on the 2019 English inspection framework, which made the curriculum the unit of inspection and forced leaders to justify their foundation subjects as rigorously as maths and English. He describes how schools discovered incoherent curriculum journeys, with repeated units and large gaps between what was planned and what was taught. History became the flagship subject because its disciplinary knowledge, how historians investigate the past and construct claims, was clear and easy to teach. The same definition fitted other subjects less well, since a musician, linguist or writer is defined more by what they make, perform or say than by how they establish claims. Hart suggests either the other subjects had not done the work or the definition is too narrow, and he sets up a short series asking whether disciplinary knowledge needs a broader definition, when to introduce it, and whether it matters in every subject.
points: The 2019 framework exposed how incoherent many primary foundation-subject curricula were, with repeated units and big gaps between plan, teaching and learning.
Subject leaders had to explain why each topic was included and how it connected to prior and later learning, which made curriculum design a leadership competence.
History worked as the model for disciplinary knowledge because school history closely mirrors the academic discipline.
The working definition, how practitioners establish claims, fits poorly for subjects defined by making, performing or saying, which suggests it may be too narrow.
Hart frames the follow-up posts around whether concepts are being mistaken for the discipline and at what age disciplinary knowledge should be introduced.
quotes: In 2019 school inspection in England shifted, making the curriculum the unit of inspection. For me and many others, the expectation of curriculum design changed almost overnight, prompting a re-examination of the national curriculum.

Curriculum narrowing was a significant finding of the inspections that led to the 2019 framework, as schools prioritised English and maths. The new framework looked at the foundation subjects in the same depth as the core.

First came the curriculum journey, and many leaders realised for the first time how incoherent their offer was: units repeated in different year groups, little material difference in expectations between years, and huge gaps between what was planned and what was taught (we ran out of time), let alone what was actually learned.

History became the flagship primary foundation subject and it was easy to see why. Disciplinary knowledge was clear and it took one article or one lecture from someone like Counsell to inspire a redesign and to do it well.

The high of history curriculum design wasn’t replicated in other subjects because the way of thinking about history didn’t quite fit. Every subject has slight variations in its logic and so the other foundation subjects weren’t as cleanly reinvigorated.
Ask the same question of a musician, a linguist or a writer, and much of the answer is about what they make, perform or say and how, rather than how they establish claims.
If a definition works beautifully in one subject but not others, there are two possible explanations. Either the other subjects haven’t done the work or the definition is too narrow.
